opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and my answer has changed over time. A few years ago I would have said the hardware is the bottleneck: robots are expensive, fragile, and hard to maintain. Those things still matter, but I've become convinced that the deeper bottleneck is on the intelligence side, and that how good the hardware needs to be depends heavily on how good the algorithms are.

One way to see this is to look at what people can do with very crude tools. A person can teleoperate a cheap arm with a simple parallel jaw gripper and do remarkable things: fold laundry, clean a kitchen, assemble a box. The hardware clearly has the physical capability. What's missing is the brain. So when people say we need much better hands or much more precise actuators before robots can be useful, I'm somewhat skeptical. Better hardware helps, but a smarter controller can compensate for a lot of hardware imperfection. Humans compensate for imprecise, noisy, compliant bodies all the time.

There are still real bottlenecks, and I'd group them into a few categories.

**Cost and reliability.** If you want robots to learn from huge amounts of real-world experience, you need many of them running for long periods without constant breakdowns. Cheaper, more robust hardware matters a lot for data collection. In a sense, the most important hardware property right now might be "can you deploy a thousand of these and have them not fall apart," more than any particular capability.

**Sensing, especially touch.** Vision has come a long way, and our models are very good at using camera images. Tactile sensing is much less mature. Good, cheap, durable touch sensors would help a lot with contact-rich manipulation. But it's a bit chicken-and-egg: you need models that can actually use tactile signals, and data that includes them, for the sensors to pay off.

**Hands and dexterity.** Dexterous hands are hard to build: they're fragile, expensive, and hard to control. I think there's a lot you can do with simpler end effectors. As the models improve, the value of more dexterous hardware goes up, because the controller can actually exploit those extra degrees of freedom.

**Onboard compute and latency.** As the models get bigger, running them fast enough for real-time control becomes a real systems challenge. You want high-frequency, reactive control, but you also want a large model that understands the world semantically. Reconciling those, by splitting computation hierarchically or doing inference efficiently on the robot, is as much a hardware and systems problem as a learning problem.

So from the algorithm designer's perspective, I'd almost flip the question. The job of the algorithms is to make the hardware requirements less stringent. If we do that well, the bottleneck becomes manufacturing and deployment at scale, which is a much better problem to have, because it's one we know how to solve. The flywheel we want is: better models make cheap robots useful, useful robots get deployed, deployment generates data, and data makes the models better. Hardware's main role in that loop is to be cheap and reliable enough to keep it spinning.

r001.rationale: It says cheaper, robust robots matter for running many robots for long periods to collect real-world experience, and describes deployment generating data.

r002.rationale: It argues that smarter controllers can compensate for hardware imperfections, but does not clearly state that current AI systems are not yet pushing hardware to its limits.

r003.rationale: It says that as models improve, the value of more capable hardware rises because controllers can exploit it, indicating AI improvements will reveal the value of hardware capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer, and this is maybe a little counterintuitive coming from someone who works on the learning side, is that I don't think hardware is the main bottleneck right now. I think the main bottleneck is the brain, not the body. If you look at the robots that exist today, the arms, the grippers, even the humanoids, they're physically capable of doing an enormous range of things that they currently can't do. A person teleoperating a fairly cheap arm with a simple two-finger gripper can fold laundry, can load a dishwasher, can do a lot of the stuff we want robots to do. So the hardware is clearly sufficient for a lot of useful tasks. What's missing is the policy that controls it.

That said, there are a few things on the hardware side that do matter a lot from an algorithms perspective, and they're maybe not the ones people usually think of. People tend to focus on things like dexterity, how many degrees of freedom does the hand have, how precise is it. And that stuff is nice, but I actually care more about reliability and cost. Because the way we make progress in learning is by collecting data and running experiments at scale, and if your robot breaks every week or costs half a million dollars, you just can't do that. So a robot that's a little bit worse but ten times cheaper and never needs maintenance is a much better research platform, and honestly probably a much better product platform too.

The other thing I'd point to is sensing. Cameras are great, they're cheap and they've gotten really good, and a lot of what we do is vision-driven. But touch is still pretty primitive. If you think about how a person manipulates something they can't see, like reaching into a bag, you're relying almost entirely on tactile feedback. Current tactile sensors are expensive, they're fragile, they're hard to integrate, and the data is not well standardized. So that's a place where better hardware would actually open up new capabilities for learning methods rather than just making existing things a bit better.

And then there's compute on the robot itself. If you want to run a large model, something that's actually doing real reasoning about the scene and the task, you either need to put a lot of compute onboard, which has power and weight implications, or you need to run it in the cloud, which has latency implications. For a lot of manipulation tasks that latency is actually fine, you don't need millisecond reactions to pick up a cup. But for some things, locomotion, catching, anything dynamic, you do. So I think over the next few years we'll see architectures that split the problem, with a fast low-level controller running onboard and a bigger model running somewhere else making higher-level decisions.

But I'd come back to the main point. If someone handed me a perfect humanoid tomorrow, with human-level dexterity and perfect sensors, I don't think we'd suddenly have capable robots. We'd have the same problem we have now, which is that we don't yet know how to get enough of the right data and train models that generalize the way a person does. That's the thing I spend my time on, because I think that's where the bottleneck actually is.

r001.rationale: It says cheaper robots make it possible to collect data and run experiments at scale.

r002.rationale: It says robots are physically capable of many tasks they cannot currently perform and identifies the controlling policy as the main bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It discusses possible hardware improvements and future compute architectures, but does not predict that AI improvements will make hardware bottlenecks clearer.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you want the robot to do. For many of the tasks that we study, the hardware is already capable of doing the task in principle. If you have a person teleoperate the robot, they can accomplish it. That’s a useful diagnostic: it tells you that the immediate bottleneck is probably the autonomy rather than the motors or the mechanical design.

But there’s a distinction between hardware that can do something once and hardware that can do it reliably for thousands of hours. From a learning perspective, reliability is enormously important. If the robot can collect experience all day, you have a very different situation than if somebody has to come in every twenty minutes and fix something. So some of the hardware improvements that would help us most are fairly unglamorous: durability, ease of maintenance, being able to run continuously.

Hands are another important example. You want dexterity, but you also want a hand that can tolerate mistakes. A learning system is going to push on things incorrectly and make bad grasps. If every mistake risks breaking a finger, that really constrains how you can learn.

And then there’s cost. Even if a cheaper robot is somewhat less capable, being able to deploy many more of them could be a huge advantage for learning. So I wouldn’t necessarily ask only, ‘What hardware gives this robot the best possible performance?’ I’d also ask, ‘What hardware lets us collect the most useful experience?’ Those can lead you to different designs.

r001.rationale: The response says cheaper robots could let researchers deploy many more units, giving them a major learning advantage by collecting more useful experience.

r002.rationale: It says that for many studied tasks, robots can already perform them when teleoperated, so the immediate bottleneck is autonomy rather than motors or mechanical design.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that AI improvements will make hardware bottlenecks clearer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the answer depends a lot on whether you mean, “What hardware would let us demonstrate something impressive?” or “What hardware would let us deploy a million robots?” For the first question, I actually think the hardware is already quite capable. The software is often the bigger limitation. We have robots that can execute very precise motions, exert substantial forces, and sense their environment reasonably well. But they still can’t reliably do many things that a person would find very easy.

For deployment, reliability and cost become much more important. A robot that works beautifully for a few hours but then requires a graduate student to fix it is a very different proposition from one that works all day in somebody’s home. And from the learning perspective, that reliability also determines how much experience you can collect. If your robot is constantly breaking, you don’t just have a maintenance problem—you have a data problem.

Hands are a particularly interesting example. You want dexterity, but you also want something robust enough to make mistakes with. Learning involves interacting with things in ways you didn’t anticipate. If every unsuccessful attempt risks damaging an expensive mechanism, that really constrains the learning process.

So I would put a lot of emphasis on robust, affordable hardware that can run for a long time with very little intervention. That might be more valuable for making progress on learning than a much more sophisticated robot that’s fragile or difficult to operate.

r001.rationale: It connects reliability to how much experience a robot can collect and calls for affordable hardware, but does not state that lower costs enable collecting more training data.

r002.rationale: It says robot hardware is already quite capable and software is often the bigger limitation, conveying that current systems are not yet pushing hardware to its limits.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that AI improvements will make hardware bottlenecks clearer.
